newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - The sin of self delusion - By E. Osborn.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - The sin of self delusion - By E. Osborn.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd

As the noted foreign correspondent Simon Barber was tempted to suggest, the human rights violations being investigated by the truth commission and the courts are nothing compared with the crime committed against South Africa's present and future generations by apartheid-era education and the resistance it fostered to learning.

Of the 41 countries willing to participate and whose results were sufficiently rigorous to be included, South Africa was stone last in the Third International Maths and Science Study - but then there was a gross underrepresentation of third world countries.
But on the other hand countries meaningfully competitive with South Africa were well represented - Singapore, Korea, Japan and other countries of the Far East.

This lies at the very heart of our industrialisation policy. Are we adequately equipped in terms of an educated and skilled manpower to withstand the open competition from countries that are so endowed?

There have been ample sound studies that have demonstrated that South Africa has been placed at a competitive disadvantage in terms of high costs of capital, because of the ongoing myopic maintenance of high real rates of interest, and of high input costs from a skewed domestic price exploitation by large upstream monopolies.
These are measurable factors.

Relatively little attention has been given to the all- important aspect of the quality and general educational level of the labour force that form the basic material that industrialists have to deal with.

Both the present and the past governments have been heavily influenced in the formulation of industrialisation policies by the static simulation studies of the Industrial Development Corporation (IDC).
I believe these to be fundamentally flawed, but I have been criticised by IDC economists as being non-professional in holding to this view.

The flaw lies in the assumption, convenient for the mathematical manipulation of the models, that competitiveness grows directly proportional to the reduction of costs and hence end-prices. Competitiveness is reduced to the simple attribute of end-price and sales volumes will grow inversely proportional to price reductions.

There is no regard for any starting differential in price in the market, nor of quality, nor of the ability of the opposition to provide greater discounts by virtue of greater volumes of production and lower unit costs of production for a host of reasons, nor of the aggressiveness of marketing of the opposition, nor of circumstances leading to widespread dumping of products of this country.
Nor is there any recognition of the overall quality of the labour that will be called upon to respond to either increased production or increased competition.

On the basis of this simple assumption of price elasticity the models clearly demonstrate, and unequivocally, that all South Africa has to do is reduce its basic costs of inputs. From this it readily follows that with trade liberalisation in the form of the reduction of tariffs there will be enhanced competitiveness for South African exports abroad and for South African producers in the domestic market.

This is delusionary but nevertheless forms the basis of South Africa's eagerness to comply with the GATT Uruguay programme of tariff reform and also is the core principle of government's macroeconomic strategy.

Of course government has not been entirely unaware of the dangers to South African industry and has devised so-called supply-side schemes of assistance designed to strengthen industry's ability to withstand competition.
But these have been generally slow in their implementation.
Thus, for example, the clothing and textile industry is again protesting the speed of the tariff reform because of the absence of the supply-side measures.
They claim that 13,000 of 17,000 jobs have been lost over the last year with the tariff phase-down, but without the implementation of supply-side measures.
Frankly, they have probably been sold a pup in being convinced that such measures will provide adequate protection.

The position of the footwear industry is little short of disastrous. The present level of output of the industry is about 30 percent below what it was in 1990 and, consequently, 6,500 jobs have been lost.

A common statement about the country's GDP is that we are consuming more than we are producing, which in other words means that there is an increasing consumption of imports relative to domestic production.

It also means that domestic industry has not grown with the rise in domestic production, which is simply a manifestation of the malaise of domestic industry under the onslaught of international competition and illegal dumping of foreign goods in the South African market.

Government has been deluding itself and us in claiming liberalisation will promote industrial development. All it is succeeding in doing is hollowing out the industrial structure that we have. And the consequences in terms of growing unemployment, crime, and social distress are all plain to us.

So a great harm is being done to the people of South Africa from self-delusion. The claims of the strategy about economic growth and employment creation are overweening because they are based on the sands of an ill-educated labour force.

The threat from the East is not going to wane. If anything, it is likely to intensify because of the pattern of single-minded development in the respective countries that has resulted in severe overcapacity.
A recent Business Week (December 2) article identifies overcapacity looming in petrochemicals, consumer appliances, passenger cars, and chips, but there are many more.

The most intense price cutting, dumping and aggressive marketing can be expected from this quarter. The only redeeming aspect, according to Business Week, is that they will run short of management skills to globalise themselves.
We need something to temper the winds of competition and a shedding of the scales of self-delusion from the eyes of government would be a good start.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
